\begin{proof}
The order of a group element is either a positive integer or infinity. If $|x|=\infty$ and $|x^{-1}|=n$ for some positive integer $n$, then
\[
 x^n=\bigl((x^{-1})^n\bigr)^{-1}=1,
\]
contradicting $|x|=\infty$. Thus $|x|=\infty$ implies $|x^{-1}|=\infty$. Applying the same argument to $x^{-1}$ gives the converse.

Now suppose $|x|=n$ is finite. Since
\[
 (x^{-1})^n=(x^n)^{-1}=1,
\]
the order of $x^{-1}$ divides $n$, so $|x^{-1}|\le n$. Applying the same argument to $x^{-1}$ gives $|x|\le |x^{-1}|$. Hence $|x|=|x^{-1}|$.
\end{proof}

Let $|x|$ denote the order of $x$. If $x$ has infinite order and $x^{-1}$ had finite order $n$, then
\[
 x^n=\bigl((x^{-1})^n\bigr)^{-1}=1,
\]
which is impossible. Therefore $x^{-1}$ also has infinite order. Conversely, applying this implication to $x^{-1}$ shows that if $x^{-1}$ has infinite order, then $x$ has infinite order.

If $x$ has finite order $n$, then
\[
 (x^{-1})^n=(x^n)^{-1}=1.
\]
Thus the order of $x^{-1}$ is at most $n$. Interchanging $x$ and $x^{-1}$ shows that the order of $x$ is at most the order of $x^{-1}$. The two orders are therefore equal.
\end{proof}

 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x^k=1,
\]
where the last equivalence follows by taking inverses. Thus $x$ and $x^{-1}$ have exactly the same positive powers that equal the identity.

\end{proof}
